questions.q: How does Neo4j expose live operational metrics on a self-hosted instance, per this lesson?
options: Via JMX, available out of the box since Neo4j runs on the JVM, and via Neo4j's built-in metrics integration for exporting to CSV, Prometheus, or Graphite
Only through the Aura console, which is unavailable to self-hosted instances
Neo4j has no way to expose operational metrics at all
Only through manually parsing the Neo4j server logs by hand
questions.explain: JMX is available by default on any self-hosted instance, and the metrics integration adds structured, production-grade export options on top of it.

questions.q: What does a healthy page cache hit ratio look like, and what does a dropping one signal?
options: It should sit consistently high, often well above 90% — a dropping or persistently low ratio signals the page cache is undersized relative to the graph's working set
It should sit near 0% for a healthy production instance
Page cache hit ratio has no relationship to Neo4j performance
A dropping page cache hit ratio always means a network problem, never a memory problem
questions.explain: This is the direct Neo4j equivalent of watching SQL Server's buffer cache hit ratio for the same underlying reason.

questions.q: What does a sudden drop in transaction throughput combined with rising latency typically point to, per this lesson, when incoming query volume hasn't dropped?
options: Contention somewhere — lock waits, an undersized page cache forcing disk I/O, or replication lag in a causal cluster
A problem with the client application's network connection only, never the database itself
This combination never has a meaningful cause worth investigating
It always means the Neo4j license has expired
questions.explain: The lesson lists these as the realistic causes worth checking first when throughput drops and latency rises together.

questions.q: When page cache hit ratio drops alongside rising transaction latency, what does this lesson say is almost always the right first fix?
options: Increase dbms.memory.pagecache.size — the same instinct as a SQL Server DBA reaching for more buffer pool memory when seeing similar symptoms
Immediately fail over to a read replica and shut down the leader
Rebuild every index in the graph regardless of whether they're being used
Switch the database to Community Edition to reduce overhead
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly connects this symptom pattern back to page cache sizing from the previous lesson, rather than something more exotic.

questions.q: What operational lifecycle does this chapter, ending with this lesson, say it has covered for a real Neo4j deployment?
options: Protect it (backup/restore), keep it available (causal clustering), make it fast (tuning), hand it off or watch it (Aura and monitoring)
Only how to write Cypher queries, with no operational content at all
Only graph data science algorithms, unrelated to operations
Only how to install Neo4j for the first time
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly frames this as the full operational lifecycle a DBA already carries for relational deployments, applied to Neo4j.
